CODEOWNERS Shadow Checker

GitHub resolves a CODEOWNERS file with the last matching pattern wins -- the same rule .gitignore uses. That means a narrow, specific rule can work perfectly for months and then silently stop winning the moment anyone adds a broader rule that also matches, anywhere below it in the file. Nothing errors. The pull requests it used to route for review just quietly stop requiring that reviewer. This tool resolves every file in your list against every rule, the same way GitHub does, and names exactly which rules are dead weight.

1. Get your CODEOWNERS file and file list (optional CLI)

Node.js, no dependencies to install. Auto-detects CODEOWNERS, .github/CODEOWNERS, or docs/CODEOWNERS, and your tracked files via git ls-files:

node cli/check.mjs

Get check.mjs and codeowners.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install, nothing sent anywhere. You do not need the CLI at all: paste your CODEOWNERS file and a plain list of paths directly into step 2 below instead.

2. Paste your CODEOWNERS file and file list

Paste your CODEOWNERS file and file list, then click Check.

Report

Rules

#PatternOwners

Files with no matching rule

Path

Common questions

What does "last match wins" actually mean?

GitHub checks a file's path against every pattern in CODEOWNERS, in file order, and the LAST pattern that matches decides who owns the file -- not the most specific one, and not the first one. This is the same rule .gitignore uses. A narrow rule near the top of the file is silently overridden the moment a broader rule that also matches gets added anywhere below it, however much later.

Why does a broad rule added later break a specific rule that already worked?

The specific rule still exists and still matches its files -- it just stops winning, because the new broad rule matches those same files and sits after it in the list. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the pull requests it used to route for review just quietly stop requiring that reviewer. This is the single most common way a CODEOWNERS file drifts from what its author intended.

How is this different from GitHub's own CODEOWNERS syntax highlighting?

GitHub's editor flags syntax errors -- an unknown user, a malformed pattern. It does not check whether a rule ever actually wins ownership of a real file in your repository, because that requires resolving every pattern against every path and comparing winners, which is exactly what this tool does against the file list you provide.

A rule shows as "unmatched" instead of "shadowed" -- what is the difference?

Shadowed means the rule matched files in your list but a later rule always overrode it -- real evidence the rule is dead weight. Unmatched means the rule matched nothing in your list at all, which usually means a typo in the pattern, a path that no longer exists, or simply a sample that did not happen to include a matching file -- so it is reported separately rather than lumped in with genuine shadowing.

Does a clean report mean my CODEOWNERS file is correct?

It means no rule in your file is dead weight against the files you listed, every owner is syntactically valid, and every listed file has a matching rule (or is flagged as uncovered). It cannot tell you an owner is a real collaborator on the repository -- that needs an authenticated GitHub API call this tool deliberately never makes -- and it can only see the files you gave it, so a file you left out of the list is not checked.

Evidence, not a determination. This resolves ownership against the file list you gave it. It cannot tell you an owner is a real collaborator on the repository -- that needs an authenticated GitHub API call this tool deliberately never makes -- and a rule matching nothing in your list is reported as a notice, not proof the pattern is wrong. Treat a clean report as evidence about this specific file list, not a guarantee the CODEOWNERS file has no other issues.

It is not legal or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified review of your repository's access controls. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use it as a system of record.

Nothing leaves your browser. The CLI reads files on your own machine and never makes a network request. The page you're reading now only parses text you paste into it locally; nothing is uploaded, and no authorisation to check a repository is needed since nothing is fetched from GitHub. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day — no CODEOWNERS content, no file paths, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

vs-reading-codeowners-by-eye.html.text:
← CODEOWNERS Shadow Checker

This checker vs. reading CODEOWNERS by eye

Reading the file yourself works fine for a short CODEOWNERS file with a handful of rules -- you can usually tell which pattern is more specific at a glance. It stops working the way most CODEOWNERS files actually grow: a specific rule (/src/payments/*.js @payments-team) is added, works for months, and then someone adds a broader rule further down the file (*.js @generalists) for an unrelated reason. Nothing about that is visible from reading top to bottom. GitHub's own syntax highlighting finds no problem either -- every pattern is valid, every owner is real. The earlier rule still matches its files; it just never wins ownership of them again, silently, under GitHub's last-match-wins resolution.

This tool does not read the file for you -- it resolves it the way GitHub actually does, every pattern against every file in your real list, and names exactly which rules never win anything because a later, broader rule always overrides them. That is a mechanical resolution problem, not a reading-comprehension one, and it is the one thing GitHub's own syntax checker does not do.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I just want to confirm my CODEOWNERS file has no syntax errors. GitHub's own editor highlighting -- that's exactly its job, and this tool checks the same syntax rule as a secondary pass.
I want to know whether an earlier, specific rule still wins ownership against my actual files, or a later rule quietly overrides it. This checker -- resolves last-match-wins against your real file list and names the exact overriding rule, instead of leaving you to trace it by eye.
I want this checked automatically in CI, with a non-zero exit on a shadowed rule. This checker's exported buildReport function -- wireable into any CI step, no GitHub API call required.
I'd rather not re-derive last-match-wins by hand every time the file changes. This checker -- paste the CLI's JSON (or the file contents and path list) into the report viewer and get the resolution done for you.

Neither replaces the other, and in practice both matter: GitHub's own highlighting for whether the file parses at all, this tool for the recurring question reading it once never answers -- whether every rule you think is protecting a path is actually still winning anything.

Try it

node cli/check.mjs

Auto-detects your CODEOWNERS file and tracked files, no reading required. Paste the JSON into the checker for the plain-English report of exactly which rules a later rule shadows.

Common questions

Should I use this tool instead of just reading the CODEOWNERS file myself?

For a short file with a handful of rules, reading it yourself is often enough -- you can usually see which pattern is more specific at a glance. This tool exists for the case that breaks that instinct: a file that has grown over months or years, where a broad rule added recently for an unrelated reason now sits below several older, specific rules and silently wins every one of them under GitHub's last-match-wins order. Nothing about that is visible from reading the file top to bottom -- it only shows up once you resolve every pattern against every file the way GitHub actually does.

Isn't this the same thing GitHub's own CODEOWNERS syntax highlighting already checks?

No, and that gap is exactly why this tool exists. GitHub's editor confirms every pattern parses and every owner is a real, well-formed reference -- it does not resolve each pattern against your actual file list and compare who wins. A CODEOWNERS file can be syntactically perfect, with GitHub's own highlighting showing no problem anywhere, while a later catch-all rule has already made an earlier, specific rule dead weight. Syntax validity and resolution correctness are two different questions, and GitHub's built-in check only answers the first.

How is this different from just grepping the file for a pattern I'm worried about?

Grepping finds the rule; it doesn't tell you whether the rule still wins anything. You'd still have to manually check every later line for a broader pattern that could override it, against every file that rule is supposed to cover -- exactly the resolution this tool automates. It reports every rule that never wins ownership of any file in your list, separately from rules that matched nothing at all, so you don't have to re-derive last-match-wins by hand for each one you're unsure about.

Is my CODEOWNERS file or file list uploaded anywhere?

No. The CLI (check.mjs) reads files already on your machine and never makes a network request -- it does not need to, since resolving CODEOWNERS needs no GitHub API call. The browser report viewer only parses text you paste into it yourself, locally in your browser. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day, with no CODEOWNERS content and no file paths in it.

Want the exact before-and-after of a rule losing its review requirement? Read why a CODEOWNERS review requirement can silently stop firing.

Evidence, not a determination. This resolves ownership against the file list you gave it. A rule matching nothing in your list is reported as a notice, not proof the pattern is wrong -- it may simply be that your list didn't include a matching file.

It is not legal or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified review of your repository's access controls. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for having authorisation to check any repository you point it at. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The CLI reads files already on your own machine and never makes a network request -- never through this site. This page only parses text you paste into it locally.

why-codeowners-review-stops-being-requir.text:
← Back to the CODEOWNERS Shadow Checker

Why a CODEOWNERS review requirement can silently stop firing

A repository has "Require review from Code Owners" turned on. For months, a change under /src/payments/*.js has correctly required the payments team's approval before it can merge. Then one day it doesn't -- the pull request opens, the payments team is not requested, and it merges without them ever seeing it. Nobody touched the payments rule. Nobody touched the payments files. The repository's own settings page still lists "Require review from Code Owners" as enabled.

What actually happened underneath

GitHub does not pick the most specific matching rule for a file, and it does not pick the first one written. It checks every pattern in the file, in order, and the last one that matches wins -- exactly the rule .gitignore uses for exclusions. Somewhere between "worked" and "stopped working", a new line was added below the payments rule -- for a completely unrelated reason, by someone who had no idea a payments rule existed: 

# Line 4 -- present since the repository was created, worked for months
/src/payments/*.js @payments-team

# Line 19 -- added later, for a different reason entirely
*.js @generalists

src/payments/charge.js still matches line 4, exactly as it always did. It now also matches line 19, which sits below it. Under last-match-wins, line 19 decides ownership. Line 4 is not broken, not removed, and not flagged by anything -- it simply never wins again, for any file it matches, from the moment line 19 landed.

Why nothing on the pull request says so

GitHub resolves CODEOWNERS the same way every time it is asked: fresh, from whatever the file currently says, with no record of who used to be the answer. Branch protection asks "who owns this file, right now" and gets a correct answer under the file as it stands -- @generalists. There is nothing wrong to report, because nothing is wrong from GitHub's side: the file is valid, every owner is real, and the resolution is exactly what last-match-wins specifies. The gap is between what the file says now and what its author intended when they wrote line 4, and that gap has no error message, because it isn't an error.

Two fixes, same effect

Move the specific rule later Put /src/payments/*.js @payments-team after *.js @generalists in the file. Both rules stay; the payments rule now sits last among the ones that match payments files, so it wins again.
Narrow the broad rule Change *.js @generalists so it no longer matches src/payments/** -- for example scoping it to a specific directory instead of the whole tree. The payments rule wins because the conflict is gone, not because of position.

Either way, the fix is a one-line edit and the failure mode does not recur for these two rules -- until a third rule broad enough to match the same files is added below both of them, which is exactly why this is worth checking after every change to the file, not just once.

Checking for it without reading the file by eye

check.mjs only gathers your CODEOWNERS file and tracked file list into JSON -- it does not itself decide pass or fail, because that judgment belongs to the browser report at index.html. To gate a CI job instead, call the same pure function the page uses, buildReport from codeowners.mjs, directly: 

import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';
import { buildReport } from './codeowners.mjs';

const codeowners = readFileSync('CODEOWNERS', 'utf8');
const paths = execFileSync('git', ['ls-files'], { encoding: 'utf8' }).split('\n').filter(Boolean);
const report = buildReport(codeowners, paths.join('\n'));

if (!report.ok) {
  console.error(`${report.shadowed.length} shadowed rule(s), ${report.syntaxErrors.length} syntax error(s)`);
  process.exit(1);
}

That is the entire dependency: one pure module, no network call, no GitHub token. It reports evidence against the file list you gave it, same as the browser page -- see the checker's own disclaimer for what that does and does not cover.

Common questions

Does branch protection notice when a CODEOWNERS rule stops winning?

No. Branch protection's "Require review from Code Owners" setting asks GitHub to resolve the file at merge time and request whichever team wins under last-match-wins. If a broader rule now wins instead of yours, GitHub asks that rule's owners -- correctly, by its own logic -- and nothing on the pull request says a different team used to be asked.

Can this happen without anyone editing the rule that stopped working?

Yes, and this is the case that is hardest to trace. The rule itself, and every file it matches, can stay exactly as they were. All that has to change is a broader pattern being added anywhere below it in the file -- for an unrelated reason, by someone who has never looked at the earlier rule and has no reason to.

If I delete the newer catch-all rule, does the older rule immediately start winning again?

Yes -- last-match-wins is recalculated fresh from the current file on every resolution, with no memory of what won before. Removing whichever later rule now matches the same files hands the win straight back to the earlier, more specific rule, with no other change needed.

Does moving the specific rule below the broad rule fix it, or does it have to be deleted?

Moving it works just as well as deleting the broad rule, and is usually the smaller edit: last-match-wins only cares about position in the file, not when each rule was written. Put the specific rule after the broad one and it wins again, with both rules still present.
